# The name Maitreya and the world it opens

A name is a door. **Maitreya** opens ​onto an entire world: the domain of future buddha, loving-kindness, a Buddhist tradition, and centuries of storytelling, worship, and scholarship. This post walks through that world room by room — the name ‌and its roots, the original script, the sound of it, the myths, the symbols, the sites, the afterlife across cultures — and ends at the newest room of all: a Unicode domain ‌that makes the whole structure addressable. *maitreya* gets you to the same building, but only the restored form tells you why it was built.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Maitreya
- **ASCII ​form:** maitreya
- **Meaning:** "'The Benevolent One' — the Bodhisattva who will return as the future Buddha"
- **Domain of influence:** Future Buddha, Loving-Kindness
- **Pantheon:** Buddhist
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form
- **Original script:** मैत्रेय (Devanagari)

## Overview

​**Maitreya** (*maitreya*) — Future Buddha, Loving-Kindness · 'The Benevolent One' — the Bodhisattva who will return as the future Buddha — belongs to the Buddhist tradition, where it is catalogued under the ​domain "Future Buddha, Loving-Kindness". The name means "'The Benevolent One' — the Bodhisattva who will return as the future Buddha".

**Maitreya** is future buddha, loving-kindness. The name means "'The Benevolent One' ​— the Bodhisattva who will return as the future Buddha" and belongs to the buddhist tradition.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Maitreya** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/maitreya/). The restoration needs ​no distinctive letters or diacritics its ASCII form would lose. The plain ASCII form *maitreya* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is ‌the form the project defends as philologically complete.

## The Name

The name is attested in Devanagari as **मैत्रेय**. Etymologically it means "'The Benevolent One' — the Bodhisattva who will return as ​the future Buddha".

The ASCII form *maitreya* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Maitreya** recovers ​the full diacritic detail of the scholarly transliteration directly in the address bar. The restoration needs no distinctive letters or diacritics its ASCII form would lose.

## The Original Script

The name is preserved in Devanagari as **मैत्रेय**.

The scholarly transliteration is *Maitreya*.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- Sanskrit Maitreya ‌is written in Devanagari as मैत्रेय
- IAST transliteration maps each Devanagari vowel and consonant to a Latin equivalent
- Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath consonants mark retroflex articulation (ṭ, ​ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

- **maitreya** — The canonical restored form Maitreya.

For the modern speaker, the ‌closest approximation is: Say "maitreya" with the stress and length implied by the scholarly restoration "Maitreya".

The ASCII form "maitreya" is a DNS compromise; the restoration "Maitreya" preserves the name's scholarly dignity.

​The pronunciation given above reconstructs the sound world in which Maitreya was invoked. Modern speakers should not expect exact identity with ancient phonology; the reconstruction is a scholarly compass, not a performance ​prescription. The restoration Maitreya keeps the prosodic information visible even when the name is typed in plain ASCII.

## Mythology

The stories of Maitreya place future buddha, loving-kindness at the center of ​a living mythological world.

### Origins (Myth)

Maitreya appears in buddhist tradition as future buddha, loving-kindness. The name's meaning, "'The Benevolent One' — the Bodhisattva who will return as the future Buddha", shapes ​the narratives told about this figure.

### Worship and Memory (Cult)

Devotees and later tradition-keepers preserved Maitreya in ritual, text, and iconography, ensuring the name survived into the modern scholarly record.

The myths ​of Maitreya survive in fragments, summaries, and later retellings. Each version reflects the interests of its tellers — poets, priests, philosophers, and scholars. The PuniCodex entry does not privilege a single ‌version; it gathers the attestations so that readers can compare them. The restoration Maitreya gives the figure a stable name around which these variants orbit.

### Metteyya at the End of the Decline ​(The Prophecy)

The oldest prophecy of the future Buddha stands in the *Cakkavattisihanāda Sutta* (DN 26): after the wheel-turning king Daḷhanemi, greed returns, human life shrinks to ten years — and then, ‌slowly, morality climbs back until people live eighty thousand years. In that age a Buddha named **Metteyya** will arise, fully awakened, attended by thousands, holding three great assemblies beneath a pavilion ​— and the wheel will turn a fourth time in this eon. Later Pāli texts place him now in **Tuṣita** heaven, where Śākyamuni himself waited before his final birth. The myth is ‌the Buddhist answer to a hard fact — every Buddha's teaching decays — and its answer is not despair but schedule: the wheel turns down and up again, and the next teacher ​is already named, already enthroned, already waiting.

### The Descent at Ketumatī (The Sanskrit Prophecy)

The Sanskrit tradition gives the future a city and a plot. The *Maitreyavyākaraṇa* — transmitted within the ‌*Divyāvadāna* and translated repeatedly into Chinese and Tibetan — describes Maitreya's birth in splendid **Ketumatī**, when the wheel-turning king **Saṅkha** rules, lifespans run to eighty thousand years, and the Dharma has been ​forgotten. Born to the brahmin Subrahma, he will leave his palace by the four gates, meet an old man, a sick man, a corpse, and a renunciant — the very sights that ‌unseated Śākyamuni — and awaken beneath a *nāga-puṣpikā* tree in a single night. The sūtra's sharpest promise is addressed to its hearers: those who receive this prophecy will meet Maitreya face ​to face. The myth makes eschatology personal — salvation not as catastrophe but as a **scheduled appointment** with a named teacher, and a ticket any listener can hold.

### The Earliest Future on ​Earth (The Cult)

Maitreya is among the very first bodhisattvas to receive cult — earlier than most of the Mahāyāna pantheon. Gandhāran art of the Kuṣāṇa centuries (2nd–3rd c. CE) already shows ‌him in the dress of a **princely ascetic**: stūpa in the crown, water flask in hand, sometimes teaching with a wheel at his feet. The emblem choice is theology in stone ‌— the stūpa names him successor, the flask the medicine of the age to come; inscriptions call him simply *Metr*, the Middle Indic form. Along the Silk Road his cult became geography: ‌caravan towns from Khotan to Dunhuang painted his descent, and devotion to his coming seeded messianic movements whenever the age grew dark — most famously in China's rebellions of the sixth and ​tenth centuries, when "Maitreya has descended" was a battle cry. The meaning of the images: a religion that put its future in human shape, standing where the caravans could see him.

## ​Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Maitreya concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **Name** — The restored form Maitreya, carrying scholarly and ‌cultural weight.
- **Domain** — Future Buddha, Loving-Kindness

Symbols function as a visual shorthand: they allow devotees and artists to recognize Maitreya across media and centuries. The attributes listed above are not decorative; ​each one encodes a claim about power, identity, or function. The restored spelling Maitreya carries the same precision in textual form.

- **The stūpa in the crown** — Gandhāran iconography crowns him ​with a small stūpa — Śākyamuni's relic-shrine marking Maitreya as the appointed successor
- **The water flask (kamaṇḍalu)** — The āmra-ghataka of the princely ascetic — the elixir of the future age, medicine ‌for a world whose Dharma has faded
- **The wheel of Dharma** — Set beneath his feet on Kushan reliefs — the teaching he will turn again, three assemblies strong
- **The nāga-puṣpikā tree** ​— The tree under which he will awaken in one night at Ketumatī — the future's Bodhi tree, named in the prophecy
- **The cloth sack (Budai)** — His Chinese transformation: the ​laughing monk with his sack of sweets, the future Buddha as abundance and belly-laugh

## Archaeology & Evidence

No monument, inscription, or artifact in the current PuniCodex corpus is yet assigned to Maitreya ‌with certainty. That absence should be read honestly: for a Buddhist name of this type the material record is expected to be thin, and the primary evidence remains the textual testimony gathered ​in the Scholarly Sources section.

Were such evidence to surface, it would take recognizable forms: votive or dedicatory inscriptions naming मैत्रेय, sanctuary or cult remains tied to future buddha and iconography matching ‌its traditional attributes (name and domain). Each candidate would be weighed against the reconstructed form of the name before entering the scholarly record.

## Realm & Domain

**Maitreya** is future buddha, loving-kindness. ​The name means "'The Benevolent One' — the Bodhisattva who will return as the future Buddha" and belongs to the buddhist tradition.

### Sacred Name

The restoration Maitreya returns the figure to scholarly ​recognition.

### Future Buddha

Central domain: future buddha, loving-kindness.

### Living Tradition

Honored in buddhist myth, cult, and cultural memory.

### Unicode Restoration

Preserved as a flagship temple despite the unregistrable plain-ASCII form.

### Maitrī, Loving-Kindness

​The name made doctrine — the first of the four brahmavihāras, boundless friendliness toward all beings.

### Tuṣita Heaven

The realm of delight where he waits — and where Śākyamuni waited before ​his own final birth.

### The Descent at Ketumatī

The Maitreyavyākaraṇa names his future city, his royal patron Saṅkha, and the tree under which he will wake.

## Across Cultures

Within the Buddhist tradition, ‌closely related names in the corpus include [[akshobhya|Akṣobhya]], [[amitabha|Amitābha]], [[amoghasiddhi|Amoghasiddhi]], [[arhat|Arhat]], [[asanga|Asanga]], and [[avalokiteshvara|Avalokiteśvara]].

Cross-cultural identifications are rarely one-to-one. Maitreya may be likened to figures in neighboring traditions without being identical to ‌them. The PuniCodex crosslink index records these resonances as relationships, not equations. The restored form Maitreya makes such comparisons possible across language boundaries.

## Cultural Legacy

Maitreya remains a touchstone for understanding ​buddhist religion, art, and identity.

The modern afterlife of Maitreya includes scholarly editions, artistic adaptations, and popular references. Each reuse renegotiates the figure’s meaning for a new audience. The PuniCodex temple participates ‌in that afterlife by ensuring that the restored name Maitreya remains findable and citable.

## A Meditation

To ‌contemplate Maitreya is to hold the idea of future Buddha, Loving-Kindness in the mind and to ask what of it endures. The name means "'The Benevolent One' — the Bodhisattva who will ‌return as the future Buddha" — and a name that carries its meaning so openly invites meditation rather than mere recollection. The tradition remembers the name as future Buddha, Loving-Kindness · ‌'The Benevolent One' — the Bodhisattva who will return as the future Buddha.

Sit with the restored form — Maitreya — and the diacritics themselves become the practice: each mark is a ‌small act of attention, a refusal to let the plain ASCII form *maitreya* stand in for the whole. What the tradition preserved in this name, the restoration asks the reader to preserve ​in turn.

## A Closer Look at the Marks

A restored name is a small map. In the case of **Maitreya**, the ‌map does not lead through diacritics or special letters, because the source tradition wrote the name in Devanagari rather than in the Latin alphabet. The ASCII form *maitreya* and the restored form ​share the same letters; the restoration is a decision about which conventional spelling should serve as the public reference.

That decision is not cosmetic. The original script attestation carries semantic and ‌phonetic information that no romanization can fully reproduce. By fixing one conventional spelling as the canonical domain form, the project prevents the drift that happens when a name is romanized differently in ‌every article, map, and database. The breakdown still lists each character — **m**, **a**, **i**, **t**, **r**, **e**, **y**, **a** — so visitors can see exactly what is being carried forward and ​what is not. What looks like "no change" is, in fact, a deliberate choice to keep the name stable, searchable, and addressable.

## Maitreya in Its Tradition

**Maitreya** does not stand alone. ​It belongs to the Buddhist tradition, where it is counted among 26 names in the PuniCodex lexicon. Its sphere — Future Buddha, Loving-Kindness — places it beside other figures who govern similar ​aspects of experience. The restored spelling is therefore not only a philological decision; it is a way of keeping the name in the company of its kin. When the address bar shows ​**Maitreya**, it marks the boundary between a generic search term and a named entry in a living catalog of myth. That catalog is the point of the project. Every restored name ‌is a vote for specificity: the web should know the difference between a figure and a keyword, between a tradition and a trend. **Maitreya** is one such vote.
